svg.title: Diagram of the Panopticon
svg.desc: Top-down plan of Jeremy Bentham's Panopticon prison: a central watch tower surrounded by a ring of individual, backlit cells, with numbered notes explaining how one-way visibility produces self-discipline in Foucault's analysis.
svg.text: The Panopticon: Bentham's Prison Plan, Foucault's Model of Power
Top-down plan of Jeremy Bentham's circular prison design (1791), as Foucault used it in Discipline and Punish (1975)
Watch
tower
Central watch tower
The observer sits here, behind blinds. Inmates can never
tell whether anyone is actually looking.
Cells around the ring
Each prisoner is alone, separated from neighbours by
walls, and fully visible from the tower.
Windows to the outside
Light enters from behind each cell, so the prisoner shows
up as a silhouette against the light.
Individualising walls
Side walls block contact between inmates: visibility for
the guard, isolation for the prisoner.
Open ring and sight lines
One watcher can, in principle, see every cell. The gaze
runs only one way.
Foucault's point
Being seen, never seeing: because you cannot know when
you are watched, you behave as if you always are.
Power becomes automatic, and people end up policing
themselves.
For Foucault the Panopticon is a model of disciplinary
power found in schools, factories, hospitals and
barracks, not only prisons.
Prisoner
Line of sight
Window / backlight
